title: Signs for those who think
hookLine: ships on the sea, rain, winds, clouds between sky and earth (2:164)
last: INNA LILLAHI WA INNA ILAYHI RAJI'UN.

lines: A CARGO SHIP SLIDES INTO HARBOR.
cards: A cargo ship, longer than a city block, slides into a harbor carrying the bananas you'll buy next week.

Over it, a weather front rolls in from the sea: a gray wall of cloud, water hanging in the air, held up by nothing you can see. Then the wind turns, rain falls on the hills behind the town, and soon the hills are green.
Ordinary things, seen so often they're barely seen. Al-Baqarah asks for another look. Today: signs for those who think.

teach.b: Verse one hundred sixty-four is a list. Count with me. The creation of the heavens and the earth.
The alternation of night and day. Ships that run on the sea with what benefits people. The water God sends down from the sky, bringing the earth to life after it was dead.
Every kind of creature scattered across it. The turning of the winds. And the clouds, held in service between sky and earth.
Seven things, and then: in these are signs for people who use their reason. Two words carry the verse. The first is ayat, signs, the same word Muslims use for the verses of the Qur'an.

teach.h: AYAH: A VERSE, AND A CLOUD
teach.b: A line of the book is an ayah, and so is a cloud; the book and the world are both read. The second is ya'qilun, those who reason.
It comes from 'aql, the mind, and the classical dictionaries connect that root to 'iqal, the cord used to tie a camel so it doesn't wander off.
To reason, in that picture, is to hold a thought still long enough to follow it. Other verses end with a similar call: for those who think, who reflect, who understand.
Faith, here, isn't asked to look away from the world. It's asked to look harder at it. Some Muslim scholars, astronomers and physicians among them, pointed to verses like this as a reason to study.

how: Muslims call both the verses of the Qur'an and the features of the natural world ayat, signs, and teachers encourage reflection, tafakkur, on rain, sky and creatures as a form of worship.

games.q: rain, wind and clouds come every week. what does verse 164 ask you to do with them?
o: read them as signs, and think.
games.why: read them: in these are signs for people who use their reason. the world is read like the book.

practice: Find a cloud, through a window or outside, and stay with it: watch its edge change, which way it moves, and how fast.
If there are no clouds, watch whatever moves, a tree in the wind, light on a wall, without naming or explaining it, the way you'd read a line slowly.

wordCard.voice: Ayah. A sign — the same word Muslims use for a verse of the Qur'an, given here to ships, rain, winds and clouds. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a sign; also a verse of the Qur'an. plural: ayat.

carryVoice: Your line: look harder at the world. A cloud can be read like a verse. See you tomorrow.
